body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Accuracy of a natural language processing triage flag for urgent patient portal messages: a validation study in primary care","authors":"Nakamura-Obi E, Fairbairn-Adeyemi T, Castellano-Hurst M","year":2023,"venue":"Journal of Primary Care Informatics","doi":"10.5555/jpci.2023.0415","providerType":"diagnostic accuracy study","abstract":"We ran an automated triage flag on 2,400 randomly sampled portal messages from four primary care practices and compared it with a reference standard of two clinicians reviewing each message independently, with a third resolving disagreements. Urgent messages made up 4 percent of the sample. Sensitivity for urgent messages was 86 percent (95 percent CI 79 to 91) and specificity was 91 percent. Sensitivity was 71 percent for messages written in languages other than English. Most missed urgent messages combined several requests, with the urgent one last. The authors caution that accuracy may differ in other patient populations."},{"title":"Patient portal message volume and physicians' after-hours work: a multi-site analysis","authors":"Lindahl-Mbeki R, Osei-Carrington J","year":2021,"venue":"Clinical Workload Research","doi":"10.5555/cwr.2021.0098","providerType":"cohort study","abstract":"We linked electronic record audit logs for 212 primary care physicians to their daily portal message counts over one year. Each additional 10 messages per day was associated with 23 minutes more work in the record outside scheduled hours. Physicians in the highest fifth of message volume reported higher burnout scores. Messages about medications and test results took longest to handle. The analysis could not separate message volume from other features of busy practices, and it did not record who wrote the messages or how urgent they were."},{"title":"Reference standards for patient message triage studies: agreement between clinicians","authors":"Okafor-Svensson L, Brandt-Kariuki A","year":2024,"venue":"Informatics Methods Notes","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Two clinicians independently rated the urgency of 900 patient portal messages without clinical context beyond the message and the problem list. Agreement on whether a message needed same-day attention was moderate (kappa 0.62). A third clinician adjudicated disagreements, which involved 14 percent of messages. Disagreement was most common for messages describing chronic symptoms that had changed, and for messages from carers. The authors recommend a written urgency definition with examples, calibration before rating, and adjudication rather than consensus discussion, and they report that rating took about one minute per message."},{"title":"Automated triage of patient messages: a systematic review of diagnostic accuracy","authors":"Petersen-Achebe K, Morrow-Tanaka S, Diallo-Whitfield C","year":2020,"venue":"Health Informatics Evidence Reviews","doi":"10.5555/hier.2020.0033","providerType":"systematic review","abstract":"We included 12 studies of automated triage of patient messages. Reported sensitivity for urgent messages ranged from 62 to 94 percent. Most studies were at high risk of bias in the reference standard, because a single clinician rated messages or raters knew the automated result. Spectrum bias was common: several studies enriched samples with obviously urgent messages. Only 2 studies were multi-site, and none reported accuracy by patient language or age. The review recommends independent double rating and random sampling."},{"title":"Clinicians' experience of managing patient portal messages: an interview study","authors":"Haddad-Lund N, Oyelaran-Pierce G","year":2022,"venue":"Primary Care Workforce Studies","doi":"10.5555/pcws.2022.0151","providerType":"qualitative research","abstract":"We interviewed 24 physicians and nurse practitioners about portal messages. Participants described answering messages in the evening, guilt about delays, and fear of missing an urgent message among routine requests. Several were cautious about automated triage and wanted to know how often it would miss urgent messages before relying on it. Participants suggested that a flag should route urgent messages to a clinician quickly rather than decide what could wait. Nurse practitioners described triaging messages for physicians without protected time, and several participants had changed their working hours to keep up with the queue."},{"title":"Language, age and the content of patient portal messages in primary care","authors":"Clinic Informatics Collaborative","year":2019,"venue":"Informatics practice report series","providerType":"report","abstract":"We described 5,000 portal messages from three clinics. Messages from patients aged over 75 more often contained several requests in one message. Messages written in languages other than English were three times as likely to be routed to the wrong staff member by reception teams. Carers wrote a fifth of messages for patients over 80. The report recommends that any automated routing be tested separately for older patients, carers and messages in languages other than English. It did not assess clinical urgency or outcomes."},{"title":"Spectrum effects in the accuracy of message triage across clinic populations","authors":"Varga-Mensah D, Olsen-Castellanos R","year":2025,"venue":"Journal of Diagnostic Informatics","doi":"10.5555/jdi.2025.0012","providerType":"diagnostic accuracy study","abstract":"We validated the same message triage flag in five clinics with different patient populations against a two-clinician reference standard. Sensitivity for urgent messages varied from 74 to 90 percent across clinics, and was lowest in the clinic with the most messages in languages other than English. Specificity varied less. Pooling clinics hid these differences. The authors recommend reporting accuracy by clinic and by message language, and sampling enough urgent messages in each clinic to do so. The reference standard was the same in every clinic."}]}
